Wentest
WENT-est
v. (2nd pers. sing., past t.)
The second-person singular past of go, formed on the old past went with the -est ending. Webster 1828 lists it among the forms used with thou. In Scripture it is nearly always used of God going forth for His people, or of His people going after Him.

Biblical Definition

Wentest is the word of a going-forth remembered, and Scripture uses it for the two goings that matter: God’s out of Seir, and Israel’s after Him into the wilderness. Deborah opens her song with the first: LORD, when thou wentest out of Seir, when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled, and the heavens dropped, the clouds also dropped water (Judges 5:4). The God of Israel is described as a warrior leaving His camp, and creation reacts. Habakkuk uses the same construction for the whole work of redemption: Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked (Habakkuk 3:13) — a going-forth aimed at a head to be wounded, which reaches back to Genesis 3:15. Jeremiah records the other direction, and it is the tenderest verse in his book: I remember thee, the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals, when thou wentest after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown (Jeremiah 2:2). God remembers Israel’s following in the desert as a bride’s devotion, and says so at the head of a chapter of indictment. And in Acts the word is a rebuke turned inside out: Thou wentest in to men uncircumcised, and didst eat with them (Acts 11:3), the charge against Peter that his account of Cornelius answered for ever.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives WENTEST as the second person singular of the past tense of the verb GO, used with thou: didst go, didst proceed, didst pass from one place or state to another.

expand to see more

WENTEST — the second person singular, past tense, of the verb GO; used with the pronoun thou.

WENT — the past tense of GO, borrowed from the obsolete verb WEND, to turn or proceed.

GO, v.i. — To move, to pass, to proceed from one place, condition, or state to another.

To go forth, in Scripture, is often said of God coming out to fight for His people or to execute judgment.

From Saxon wendan, to turn or wend, whence the past went supplied the missing past of go.

Key Scripture

Judges 5:4 — "LORD, when thou wentest out of Seir, when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled, and the heavens dropped, the clouds also dropped water."

Habakkuk 3:13 — "Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck. Selah."

Jeremiah 2:2 — "Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying, Thus saith the LORD; I remember thee, the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals, when thou wentest after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown."

Acts 11:3 — "Saying, Thou wentest in to men uncircumcised, and didst eat with them."

Modern Corruption

Acts 11:3 records the church’s first attempt to make a cultural boundary into a gospel boundary, and every later version of the same instinct — whichever direction it runs — is answered by the way Peter replied.

expand to see more

The charge against Peter was not doctrinal in form. Thou wentest in to men uncircumcised, and didst eat with them — a complaint about table fellowship, which is exactly where such disputes always surface. Peter’s answer is a narrative: the sheet let down, the voice, the three men at the gate, and then the decisive fact, the Holy Ghost fell on them, as on us at the beginning. His conclusion is a question: what was I, that I could withstand God? The apostolic settlement is that God’s giving of the Spirit determines who belongs, and no cultural marker may be added to it. That principle cuts in every direction, against the congregation that would keep out the poorly dressed and the recently converted as firmly as against the party at Jerusalem.

Jeremiah 2:2 supplies the pastoral counterweight, and it is worth dwelling on. God begins a chapter of severe indictment by remembering aloud what Israel was like at first: the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals, when thou wentest after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown. He recalls the following before He names the forsaking, and He calls it love. That is how God speaks of a people He is about to charge with two great evils. It is a rebuke to the corrupted pastoral instinct that treats a declining believer’s earlier devotion as evidence it was never real; God does not, and Revelation 2:4 makes the same move with Ephesus — thou hast left thy first love presupposes that the first love was genuine.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yatsa (H3318), to go out, to go forth; halak (H1980), to go, to walk; tsaad (H6805), to march, to step; Greek eiserchomai (G1525), to go in, to enter.

expand to see more

Hebrew yatsa (H3318) — to go out, go forth; used of the LORD going out to war (Judges 5:4; Habakkuk 3:13).

Hebrew halak (H1980) — to go, to walk; when thou wentest after me in the wilderness (Jeremiah 2:2).

Hebrew tsaad (H6805) — to step, to march; when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom.

Greek eiserchomai (G1525) — to go in, to enter; the charge in Acts 11:3 is that Peter went in.

Hebrew kelulah (H3623) — espousals, betrothal; the love of thine espousals (Jeremiah 2:2).

Usage

"LORD, when thou wentest out of Seir (Judges 5:4) — God described as a warrior leaving His camp."

"Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people (Habakkuk 3:13) — a going-forth aimed at a head to be wounded."

"When thou wentest after me in the wilderness (Jeremiah 2:2) — God remembering a bride’s following before naming her sin."
